On the evening of February 15, 1898, the USS Maine exploded and sank in Havana harbor. More than 250 members of her crew died as a result. Captain Charles Sigsbee commanded the ship at the time of the explosion; in other words, the officer answerable for her when she blew up was Sigsbee, and his testimony shaped every later inquiry. Every investigation that followed turned on a single question: did the first blast come from outside the ship or from within her? The two answers are mutually exclusive. Either the initial explosion that destroyed the Maine originated outside the hull, or it originated inside the hull. One of them must be true, and they cannot both be.

The first official answer came quickly. Captain William T. Sampson presided over the 1898 naval court of inquiry, which met while war fever was rising in the United States. Its central physical evidence came from divers working in murky water. They reported that part of the Maine's forward keel had been bent upward into an inverted V shape. The court read that distortion as the mark of force driven up from below the ship. Contemporary engineers had already raised spontaneous combustion in the coal bunkers as a known hazard on steel warships. Even so, the court did not adopt the coal-fire explanation. It concluded that a submarine mine had caused the destruction of the Maine. Because the court could not identify who placed such a mine, its finding fed public anger at Spain rather than closing the technical question.

The wreck lay in the harbor for more than a decade. In 1911 a second naval board under Rear Admiral Charles Vreeland examined it, after engineers had built a cofferdam around the hull and drained it. This gave investigators a far clearer view than the 1898 divers ever had. The Vreeland board dated the bent keel to a different section of the ship than the Sampson court had. It still ultimately concluded that an external explosion beneath the hull had set off the Maine's forward magazines. That finding is evidence that the forward magazines detonated, a point no investigator has seriously disputed. Their detonation caused the catastrophic explosion that sank the ship, and through it the heavy loss of life. Even so, the debris alone cannot fully settle how the magazines were set off. At least one of two things happened: the magazines exploded, or an external explosive charge detonated against the Maine's bottom plating, perhaps both. The Vreeland board held that both occurred, with the outside charge triggering the magazines.

The most rigorous reassessment came from outside the regular chain of naval boards. Admiral Hyman Rickover, prompted by renewed interest in the disaster, assembled specialists in explosives and naval engineering. They went back to the 1898 and 1911 records and photographs. Rickover's 1976 study, published as "How the Battleship Maine Was Destroyed," judged that the plating damage matched an internal blast pushing outward. It found no sign of the shock a mine would have produced, and noted that no mine of the period could plausibly have caused such deformation. It proposed that heat from spontaneous combustion in a coal bunker next to a forward magazine had ignited the powder.

Rickover's analysis therefore came down on the internal side of the alternative that every inquiry had faced. Later studies, including a 1998 computer modeling effort, have reopened the possibility of a mine without disproving the bunker-fire hypothesis. What the century of investigation shows most clearly is how much each verdict depended on the evidence its authors could see. It also depended on the political climate in which they were asked to deliver it.

Their detonation caused the catastrophic explosion that sank the ship, and through it the heavy loss of life. Even so, the debris alone cannot fully settle how the magazines were set off. The magazines exploded. An external explosive charge detonated against the Maine's bottom plating. The Vreeland board held that both occurred, with the outside charge triggering the magazines.

The most rigorous reassessment came from outside the regular chain of naval boards. Admiral Hyman Rickover, prompted by renewed interest in the disaster, assembled specialists in explosives and naval engineering. They went back to the 1898 and 1911 records and photographs. Rickover's 1976 study, published as "How the Battleship Maine Was Destroyed," judged that the plating damage matched an internal blast pushing outward. It found no sign of the shock a mine would have produced, and noted that no mine of the period could plausibly have caused such deformation. It proposed that heat from spontaneous combustion in a coal bunker next to a forward magazine had ignited the powder.

Rickover's analysis therefore came down on the internal side of the alternative that every inquiry had faced. Later studies, including a 1998 computer modeling effort, have reopened the possibility of a mine without disproving the bunker-fire hypothesis. What the century of investigation shows most clearly is how much each verdict depended on the evidence its authors could see. It also depended on the political climate in which they were asked to deliver it.
